items.title: Launch Preview: Falcon 9, ZhuQue-2E to launch during quiet week
items.originalTitle: Launch Preview: Falcon 9, ZhuQue-2E to launch during quiet week
items.summary: This week features a relatively quiet launch manifest, with SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9 comprising much of the launch schedule. Three Falcon 9 missions will launch a cargo resupply mission to the International Space Station, a batch of satellites for SpaceX’s Starlink constellation, and a classified set of satellites for the United States Space Force. Furthermore, a Chinese ZhuQue-2E will launch an unknown payload to orbit. Falcon 9 | Starlink Group 15-25 The first scheduled launch of the week was a Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base (VSFB) in California.

evidenceRecords.text: This week features a relatively quiet launch manifest, with SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9 comprising much of the launch schedule.

Three Falcon 9 missions will launch a cargo resupply mission to the International Space Station, a batch of satellites for SpaceX’s Starlink constellation, and a classified set of satellites for the United States Space Force.
Furthermore, a Chinese ZhuQue-2E will launch an unknown payload to orbit.
Falcon 9 | Starlink Group 15-25 The first scheduled launch of the week was a Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base (VSFB) in California.
After liftoff from SLC-4E, Falcon 9 took a southeast trajectory and landed atop SpaceX’s autonomous droneship, Of Course I Still Love You , in the Pacific.
Falcon 9 is a 3.9 m-diameter, 70 m-tall two-stage rocket.
Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy were the first orbital rockets to achieve regular re-use, with one Falcon booster having flown as many as 37 flights.

Falcon 9 | CRS-35 A Falcon 9 launch from Cape Canaveral is now much less common following the transfer of Starlink launch duties to Starship; however, International Space Station (ISS) mission orbital mechanics fit well with east coast launch sites.
One such Falcon 9 mission was CRS-35, which launched on Tuesday, Oct. 13, at 6:33 AM EDT (10:33 UTC).
ZhuQue-2E | Unknown Payload A Chinese ZhuQue-2E rocket, developed by Landspace, is scheduled to launch on Wednesday, Oct. 14, at 11:40 UTC.
ZhuQue-2E will liftoff from Site 96A at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in China, with the launch window extending to 12:19 UTC.
Following launch, ZhuQue-2E will fly due south out of Jiuquan to deploy an unknown payload to an unknown orbit.

items.title: LaNeve to industry: ‘We are not walking away from modernization’
items.originalTitle: LaNeve to industry: ‘We are not walking away from modernization’
items.summary: The U.S. Army’s top officer sought to reassure industry leaders that the service remains committed to modernization and autonomous systems, announcing a new name for the command charged with shaping the future force during remarks at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C. Christopher LaNeve said that the Futures and Concepts Command has been redesignated as U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army’s top officer sought to reassure industry leaders that the service remains committed to modernization and autonomous systems, announcing a new name for the command charged with shaping the future force during remarks at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C.
Christopher LaNeve said that the Futures and Concepts Command has been redesignated as U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM.

The change comes as the Army aligns its weapons purchases, force structure and training around new “How the Army Fights” guidance, which was published last week and explains how the service intends to wield land power in future wars.
“We are not walking away from modernization,” LaNeve said, addressing the industry partners directly at one point in his speech.

“We are sprinting towards, it,” he said, adding “and we are doing so responsibly with a recognition that resources are not endless.” LaNeve has charged FASCOM with developing corps-level autonomous capabilities through experimentation and testing.

According to a Tuesday release, the three-star command will have “capability-based formations centered on autonomous long-range fires, protection, tanks, logistics and obstacle breaching,” and will include some of the Army’s first 390A Robotic Technicians , which were activated this month.

“This goes beyond drones,” LaNeve said in the release, “FASCOM will pioneer operational concepts that harness autonomous capabilities across all warfighting functions.” The Army has come under fire recently after shuttering its experimental drone battalion in Europe less than a year after launching the novel unit to test how such a formation could operate.

evidenceRecords.text: NASA astronaut Christina Koch stands inside Kennedy Space Center’s Vehicle Assembly Building on July 14, 2021, in front of the agency’s Space Launch System (SLS) rocket that ultimately powered the Orion spacecraft on the Artemis I mission.
Koch later served as a crew member on the Artemis II mission in 2026, and on Oct. 13, 2026, NASA announced she will serve next as the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer.

NASA/Glenn Benson NASA engineer and astronaut Christina Koch will serve as the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer beginning on Sunday, Nov. 1, following the retirement of Katherine Van Hooser, who will conclude more than 35 years of distinguished service to the agency on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
In her new role, Koch will help lead NASA’s engineering community, supporting technical oversight, mission readiness, and engineering excellence across the agency’s programs and projects.
With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments.
“Christina has seen NASA engineering from both sides of the equation: developing complex systems on the ground and trusting them with her life in space,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

“After spending nearly a year living and working aboard the International Space Station and helping lead America back around the Moon on Artemis II this year, she brings an extraordinary combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and judgment to this role.

I am excited to see the impact she will have across NASA as we return Americans to the lunar surface, build the Moon Base, get underway on nuclear power in space, and develop the capabilities that will ultimately take us on to Mars.” “Katherine has been an extraordinary leader throughout her career, bringing technical expertise, sound judgment, and an unwavering commitment to mission success to some of NASA’s most complex engineering challenges,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA associate administrator and chief engineer.
“Her leadership has strengthened our engineering community and helped guide the agency through critical milestones and transitions.
As Marshall’s chief engineer and, since 2023, NASA’s deputy chief engineer, Van Hooser provided critical technical leadership and oversight across the agency’s programs.

items.summary: Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco. The attacks on both sides were a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces.

evidenceRecords.text: Civilians warned to leave target area near Sana’a before attacks as conflict between Riyadh and Houthi forces escalates Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco.
The attacks on both sides were a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces.

Before its offensive on Tuesday, a Saudi spokesperson warned civilians to leave the target area, in an apparent attempt to strike fear into the local population before the biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure.
Houthi attacks on airports and energy facilities are putting Saudi Arabia under pressure.
Could a Saudi-led international military offensive succeed against the Iran-aligned Houthi militia in Yemen?

Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco.

The Central Sabaha Station oil depot on the western side of the city contains large tanks that often hold substantial quantities of fuel derivatives, although the Yemeni Oil Company said its storage facilities were empty at the time of the attack.

Houthi oil depots at the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah, the subject of Israeli attacks in 2024, were also struck in 10 waves of attacks apparently aimed at immobilising the Houthi army as it continues its push south, including towards the city of Taiz.
Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in the Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen.
The strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthi attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left 300 injured.
The airport is closed until Saturday at the earliest, a blow to an economy that is trying to show its security makes the country a safe place to invest.
The incident underlined how Saudi Arabia has complete air dominance over Yemen while the Houthis have to reply using drones and missiles which can be intercepted.
Baraa Shiban, a Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), warned “Saudi Arabia is struggling to respond to the Houthi’s improved arms technology.
Until relatively recently Houthi missiles and drones fell in desert areas or if they got through were intercepted.
They have learned how to deploy drones that fly lower and are smaller, and are less easy to detect.

items.title: Anduril reveals family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles
items.originalTitle: Anduril reveals family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles
items.summary: Anduril released a new family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles in an effort to create a more diverse range of defensive measures while building at scale. Steelfin, a family of highly configurable, mass-producible, surface-to-air interceptor missiles, has been developed to deliver cost, volume and capability across a variety of threats, according to a release .

evidenceRecords.text: Anduril released a new family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles in an effort to create a more diverse range of defensive measures while building at scale.

Steelfin, a family of highly configurable, mass-producible, surface-to-air interceptor missiles, has been developed to deliver cost, volume and capability across a variety of threats, according to a release .

Steefin uses a two-stage architecture compatible with different fielded designs, allowing the defense company to configure interceptor performance while reusing the same parts, production processes, and design across its family of interceptors.
The missile has a two-stage design with a booster and terminal interceptor, the release states.
The first-stage booster can accommodate various solid rocket motor boosters to meet a set range, performance, booster types, launch configurations or packing density requirements.
The second stage terminal interceptor shares the same baseline airframe, avionics, software, flight control system and interfaces across all Steelfin variants.
“Steelfin delivers a diversity of effects to meet a diversity of threats,” the release says.

“Unlike legacy missiles that carry fixed, inflexible designs that are resistant to change, Steelfin offers a common interceptor architecture that produces a family of interceptor missiles, each of which can be configured for a specific mission.” The interceptor family was built to address threats across the air-and-missile defense spectrum, such as point defense, integrated air and missile defense and ballistic missile defense, while aiming to come at a fraction of the cost of other interceptors in mission classes.

To address issues with manufacturing volume and high demand, Anduril expects to “surge” production for any Steelfin variant by moving the interceptor through the same production line, with the same tooling, techniques and facilities, since they share a common architecture and components.
Anduril anticipates producing several thousand Steelfin variants per year in the short term, the announcement says.
Steelfin is meant to be able to integrate with any fielded fire control software systems, like AEGIS and IBCS, to ensure it fits into established battle management processes and procedures.

items.title: US Army assesses Trust Automation’s integrated drone defence system
items.originalTitle: US Army assesses Trust Automation’s integrated drone defence system
items.summary: Trust Automation has completed a US Army operational assessment of its Small-Unmanned Air Defense System (SUADS) during a National Training Center rotation at Fort Irwin, California. Conducted with the 703rd Brigade Support Battalion, 2nd Armored Brigade Combat Team, 3rd Infantry Division, the assessment evaluated SUADS in a large-scale combat operations training environment under ongoing uncrewed aerial system (UAS) threats.

evidenceRecords.text: Trust Automation has completed a US Army operational assessment of its Small-Unmanned Air Defense System (SUADS) during a National Training Center rotation at Fort Irwin, California.

Conducted with the 703rd Brigade Support Battalion, 2nd Armored Brigade Combat Team, 3rd Infantry Division, the assessment evaluated SUADS in a large-scale combat operations training environment under ongoing uncrewed aerial system (UAS) threats.

During the rotation, Trust Automation’s SUADS detected and engaged UAS between approximately two and six kilometres away, with potential coverage extending to approximately seven kilometres under favourable conditions, the company said in a 12 October press release.
Trust Automation’s integrated system combined radar, electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) sensors, NINJA and DroneBuster technologies.
SUADS brings multiple sensors and effectors into a single integrated system while enabling individual technologies to be added or upgraded as capabilities and threats evolve.
Trust Automation is also developing a mobile SUADS variant to support tactical units where forces move frequently.
For more information Trust Automation The September issue of the 2026 Unmanned Airspace Global Counter-UAS Systems Directory is now available.

items.title: Lockheed eyes fresh PAC-3 interceptor production options for Ukraine, Europe
items.originalTitle: Lockheed eyes fresh PAC-3 interceptor production options for Ukraine, Europe
items.summary: Lockheed Martin is weighing new industry partnerships to produce urgently needed PAC-3 Patriot interceptors in Europe, an avenue that could also help fill Ukraine’s shortfalls, a company executive said. Discussions about producing more Patriot interceptors outside the United States have picked up steam since Ukrainian leaders said over the summer they were promised by the Trump administration a license to make them in Ukraine to defend against Russian missile and drone barrages.

evidenceRecords.text: Lockheed Martin is weighing new industry partnerships to produce urgently needed PAC-3 Patriot interceptors in Europe, an avenue that could also help fill Ukraine’s shortfalls, a company executive said.

Discussions about producing more Patriot interceptors outside the United States have picked up steam since Ukrainian leaders said over the summer they were promised by the Trump administration a license to make them in Ukraine to defend against Russian missile and drone barrages.
U.S. government officials are still expected to make a decision, which could entail the production of PAC-2 interceptors, made by Raytheon, or Lockheed’s PAC-3.

“From a PAC-3 perspective, we’re absolutely willing to talk to Ukraine,” Jason Reynolds, vice president and general manager of the company’s integrated air and missile defense division, told Defense News in an interview at the Association of the United States Army annual convention in Washington, DC.

Patriot interceptor deliveries to Poland will be delayed, top general says “It’s really a matter of what’s their industrial capability, what’s the parts availability, those types of things,” he continued.

“It might be something like an ACE, as opposed to an MSE, that we would start with for Ukraine.” Lockheed announced development of an ACE variant during the summer, billing it as a cheaper option against relatively simple threats — at half the cost of an MSE missile designed to go against sophisticated missiles.

The new interceptor will make do with a single-pulse motor, compared with a dual-pulse of the MSE interceptor, and utilize a blast fragmentation warhead, versus the direct hit-to-kill mechanics of the MSE missile.
Reynolds cautioned that setting up interceptor missile production of whatever variant in Ukraine comes with the risk of Russian attacks on the plant.

“If we can get that started, get the supply chain started and then migrate to Ukraine as an option, that would make a lot of sense to me.” Germany is among the countries where leaders have offered to host PAC-3 production .

For an eventual PAC-3 production, Lockheed is considering partnering with Diehl Defence, with which there is a cooperation agreement on interceptor parts in place dating from October 2025, Reynolds said.

However, what we’ve seen is, with the environment as it is, everything that we produce as a capable counter-UAS system tends to get deployed somewhere,” said Kirk Williams, chief engineer at the U.S. Army Directed Energy Project Office.
In September, the Army awarded AeroVironment a $464.8 million contract for LOCUST X3, its modular, palletized high-energy laser system.
Earlier generations of the LOCUST system are actively fielded in operational environments, including at the U.S. southern border, according to AeroVironment.

That would be a great win for the Army.” It is unclear where the first high-energy counter-drone weapons under H-ELS will be deployed.

The counter-drone E-HEL contract is for more than 26 laser weapons units total, according to AeroVironment vice president of Directed Energy, John Garrity, who indicated the initial system is on target for 2027 delivery.
“We would love to be able to keep the first unit off the line for our testing and training.
The goal is to push it through testing, validation, verification and “give it to soldiers as soon as possible,” said Brig.

items.title: Army plans ‘rodeo’ to round up supply-chain problems
items.originalTitle: Army plans ‘rodeo’ to round up supply-chain problems
items.summary: The U.S. Army is planning a \"rodeo\" to round up problems that slow the deployment of new weapons, and rope in new ways to improve supply chains and make parts in more places, the service\u2019s acting chief said today.\u00a0 \u201cWe need to strain the nation's larger industrial base. We're going to stress-test the supply chain, the manufacturing processes, and see where it breaks,\u201d Adam Telle said at the Association of the U.S. Army\u2019s annual conference in Washington, D.C. Production bottlenecks and a lack of suppliers for many key parts have plagued the Army for decades.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army is planning a "rodeo" to round up problems that slow the deployment of new weapons, and rope in new ways to improve supply chains and make parts in more places, the service’s acting chief said today.

The U.S. Army is planning a \"rodeo\" to round up problems that slow the deployment of new weapons, and rope in new ways to improve supply chains and make parts in more places, the service\u2019s acting chief said today.\u00a0
\u201cWe need to strain the nation's larger industrial base.

We're going to stress-test the supply chain, the manufacturing processes, and see where it breaks,\u201d Adam Telle said at the Association of the U.S. Army\u2019s annual conference in Washington, D.C.
Production bottlenecks and a lack of suppliers for many key parts have plagued the Army for decades.
The Government Accountability Office, among others, has detailed many breaking points.

But, Telle said, those reports don\u2019t capture how bad the problem could become as the Army seeks new drones and counterdrone weapons with components made by companies far from the service\u2019s control.
For instance, he said, the Army needs to \u201cmake millions\u201d of one-way attack drones.\u00a0
\u201cIt may look simple, but it's a flying supply chain.
If somebody else controls one part, they can break the whole thing,\u201d the acting chief said.
Parts for such drones are largely made in China, which uses its market dominance to help other autocratic states like Russia and Iran attack U.S. forces and partner militaries in Europe.\u00a0
Telle, who did not name any adversary, said that \u201can economy that's an extension of the national-security apparatus\u201d can be \u201cruthlessly efficient\u201d in deploying weapons.\u00a0

The acting Army chief listed steps the Pentagon has taken to overcome bureaucratic sluggishness in developing and deploying new technologies, such as pushing more acquisition authority down to battalion-level commanders, getting more self-sustained power on U.S. bases, and introducing a program to allow private companies to test new weapons on U.S. Army ranges.

NASA/JPL-Caltech The testing team moves Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 through a hallway to the 25-Foot Space Simulator at JPL.
The corridor features photos of the historic spacecraft that have been tested in the facility since the 1960s, from the Ranger program to NASA’s Europa Clipper.

NASA/JPL-Caltech A commercial lander that will be at the forefront of NASA’s efforts to establish a Moon Base, humanity’s first lunar outpost, has passed a series of critical tests at the agency’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.
Results show that Voyager Technologies’ Griffin Mission One (Griffin-1) spacecraft is ready to survive the rigors of space exploration.
“NASA JPL’s Environmental Test Laboratory has been putting robotic explorers to the test since the Ranger program gave us NASA’s first up-close views of the Moon’s surface in the mid-1960s.

Long foam spikes that absorb sound waves and electromagnetic waves cover the walls of a specialized anechoic chamber at JPL where Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 underwent electromagnetic interference and electromagnetic compatibility testing.

NASA/JPL-Caltech Griffin-1’s testing journey Testing began in July after the 2,789-pound (1,265-kilogram) spacecraft took a cross-country road trip from Voyager Lunar Systems’ manufacturing facilities in Pittsburgh to JPL in the San Gabriel Mountain foothills.

Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 lunar lander spins on a special table in a test to measure its mass properties, which enables engineers to look for any unexpected wobbles as they assess how the vehicle will move through space.

“This spacecraft represents a new era of commercial lunar exploration, where missions like Griffin-1 are laying the groundwork for the Moon Base and helping turn sustained lunar exploration from a vision into a reality.” After proving its mettle at JPL, Griffin-1 has returned to Voyager Lunar Systems’ facility for final assembly.

evidenceRecords.text: General Dynamics Land Systems is showcasing a 1/8 model of the Wolf XM30, the company’s candidate to replace the M2 Bradley, along with PERCH 2.0, M-SHORAD Increment 4 and the F600 Leonidas at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting this week.
The Wolf is one of two vehicles competing in the Army’s XM30 program , with American Rheinmetall delivering its first Lynx XM30 prototype to the Army in September.

Retired Army officer Scott Taylor, General Dynamics Land Systems’ director of U.S. growth, told Military Times that the Bradley has reached the limits of its ability to accommodate additional capabilities and weight.
The Wolf is designed with greater capacity in mind, while improving fightability, lethality and survivability, Taylor said.
General Dynamics Land Systems delivered its first Wolf prototype to the Army in August.
PERCH 2.0 allows M1A2 Abrams main battle tanks and Stryker vehicles to launch Switchblade 300 loitering munitions while keeping operators under armor.
One PERCH 2.0 prototype has been provided to the Army for experimentation, with three more on the way.
Soldiers with 2nd Battalion, 12th Cavalry Regiment, 1st Brigade Combat Team, known as “Thunder Horse,” are currently testing the prototype at Fort Hood, Texas, Taylor noted.

The system grew out of General Dynamics Land Systems’ development of PERCH 1.0, which the company developed in less than four months after senior Army leaders discussed observations from the war in Ukraine during a 2025 event, Taylor said.
The Army initially experimented with Switchblade 600 before asking the company to focus on the smaller Switchblade 300, according to Taylor.

General Dynamics Land Systems continued developing PERCH 2.0 with its own independent research and development funding before the Army contracted for three additional prototypes under the Abrams program office.
The Army will evaluate the design after the experimentation and could compete the capability or purchase it, depending on the results, Taylor explained.

evidenceRecords.text: WARSAW, Poland — Norway’s Kongsberg has decided to build a new production facility for counter-drone systems in northern Poland, with plans to invest more than 200 million zloty ($51 million) in the plant.
The investment is connected to the company’s cooperation with Polish state-run defense group PGZ to deliver the San anti-drone system to the Polish military.
“We have been present in Poland for many years.

We think it’s important that we establish local sites in Poland,” Eirik Lie, the president and CEO of Kongsberg, told Defense News at the Warsaw Security Forum here on Oct. 12. “We are on good track for deliveries on the San program.
But also, we expect export contracts, so this enables us to be prepared for these exports from Poland.”

Under the San deal, valued at around PLN 15 billion ($3.8 billion), Kongsberg and PGZ are to supply 18 anti-drone batteries, 52 firing platoons, 18 command platoons, and 703 vehicles to the Polish military, according to data from Poland’s Ministry of National Defence.
The contract will be largely financed by loans that Poland has secured from the European Union’s Security Action For Europe (SAFE) scheme.
In a statement, the Norwegian group said it plans to sign a construction contract by the end of 2026 and begin work immediately afterward.
Serial production of counter-drone systems could begin in the first half of 2028.
The investment is expected to create more than 100 jobs in Poland once the plant reaches full capacity.

items.title: BAE Systems unveils new layered air-defense system
items.originalTitle: BAE Systems unveils new layered air-defense system
items.summary: BAE Systems unveiled new layered air-defense systems designed to counter missiles and drones on Monday at the annual meeting of the Association of the United States Army. The international defense company introduced the Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System, or MDACS, and the High-Power Microwave, or HPM, as complementary systems for protecting critical installations and field units.

evidenceRecords.text: BAE Systems unveiled new layered air-defense systems designed to counter missiles and drones on Monday at the annual meeting of the Association of the United States Army.

The international defense company introduced the Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System, or MDACS, and the High-Power Microwave, or HPM, as complementary systems for protecting critical installations and field units.

Travis Langer, BAE Systems’ communication manager, explained to Military Times that the systems together fill a capability gap created by evolving technological threats and the military’s traditional procurement process.

“Both products complement existing air defense systems, but each offer a more cost-effective solution for defense against high-volume, low-cost threats allowing the preservation of high-value missiles for the most critical targets, which extends the life and effectiveness of the entire missile stockpile,” Langer said.

The Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System According to BAE Systems, MDACS forms the kinetic layer of the defensive shield, using precision-guided munitions called Hypervelocity Projectiles, or HVPs, for both offensive and defensive operations.

“It fills a gap that traditional artillery cannot, providing a scalable layer of protection that complements existing high-tier systems,” Langer said, adding that it allows the Defense Department “to maintain a sustainable defense without draining the budget on every single engagement.” He explained MDACS combines high-accuracy guidance with the extreme velocity of the HVP.
BAE Systems secured an Army agreement to develop a prototype of MDACS in January 2025, according to reports .
The High-Power Microwave BAE Systems describes its HPM system as a “scalable directed energy weapon” built with an emphasis on affordability.
Although the system remains in the prototype stage, BAE Systems said it has reached Technology Readiness Level 6, or TRL 6.
Layered air-defense Langer explained that the two systems are not specifically designed to be used together, but they could complement each other if the mission set requires it.

items.title: Drone carrying M250 machine gun completes firing test
items.originalTitle: Drone carrying M250 machine gun completes firing test
items.summary: A heavy-duty quadcopter carrying Sig Sauer’s new M250 light machine gun has completed a test requiring it to identify and engage targets from the air, the company announced Tuesday. Sig Sauer completed the test in concert with Israel Aerospace Industries, maker of the Fire Storm 250, a reusable drone that can stay airborne for two hours and is designed with a stabilized machine-gun mount.

evidenceRecords.text: A heavy-duty quadcopter carrying Sig Sauer’s new M250 light machine gun has completed a test requiring it to identify and engage targets from the air, the company announced Tuesday.

Sig Sauer completed the test in concert with Israel Aerospace Industries, maker of the Fire Storm 250, a reusable drone that can stay airborne for two hours and is designed with a stabilized machine-gun mount.

According to a Tuesday announcement from the companies, the test required the system to hover over a simulated battlefield, ID targets with an onboard camera and fire on them using both single-shot and semi-automatic firing modes “from varying distances and altitudes.” It’s a fast development timeline for the drone, which was first unveiled last October.

The system, as Janes reported, incorporates Sig’s micro-remote-controlled weapon system along with the M250, a version of which is set to replace the Army’s M249 squad automatic weapon as part of the service’s Next-Generation Squad Weapon program.
“We’re proud of the new SIG SAUER M250, which is combat-proven technology.

It is a belt-fed platform with greater range than legacy systems and weight savings that not only provide squad-level benefits but also make drone capabilities possible.” Sig Sauer executives told Military Times earlier this month that fielding for the M250 is expected to begin in the first half of next year.

items.originalTitle: Phantom Defense acquires Karakurt and integrates net launchers into C-UAS range
items.summary: Ukrainian defence technology company Phantom Defense has announced the completion of its acquisition of the developer of Karakurt net launchers. The transaction involves the full acquisition of the business and its team. The Karakurt net deployment system enables the physical interception of uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) without kinetic impact. The device deploys a net over the target, entangling its rotors and preventing further flight. Enemy drones can be brought down in a condition suitable for examination or potential reuse in combat operations by Ukraine’s defence forces.

The post Phantom Defense acquires Karakurt and integrates net launchers into C-UAS range first appeared on Unmanned airspace .
The transaction involves the full acquisition of the business and its team.
The device deploys a net over the target, entangling its rotors and preventing further flight.
Enemy drones can be brought down in a condition suitable for examination or potential reuse in combat operations by Ukraine’s defence forces.
The systems are adapted for different carrier platforms and tactical scenarios.
For DJI Mavic, Matrice and Autel platforms (M3, M4, A4 variants), the system deploys a net vertically from above.
For FPV drones and specialised platforms, the system uses forward net deployment with a target retention mechanism to intercept moving targets at high speed.
Phantom Defense says military units have deployed more than 50,000 Karakurt kits over the past six months.

To collect operational data and further improve the technology, the company has introduced a programme offering free replacement of consumables to units that submit video evidence of successful enemy UAS interceptions.
The programme has already recorded more than 5,000 video-confirmed interceptions.
Building on the acquisition, Phantom Defense is introducing MANGAL, a close-range UAS net interception system integrated into its counter-UAS ecosystem.

items.originalTitle: Anduril awarded contract to expand US Army’s next-gen battlefield command system
items.summary: The Army awarded Anduril Industries a contract on Sept. 30 worth up to $1.8 billion over five years to help the service transition its new battlefield software from the experimentation phase to the fielding phase. Anduril previously helped develop the prototype for the service’s Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, for the 4th Infantry Division, using its proprietary AI-powered operating system Lattice.

evidenceRecords.text: The Army awarded Anduril Industries a contract on Sept. 30 worth up to $1.8 billion over five years to help the service transition its new battlefield software from the experimentation phase to the fielding phase.

Anduril previously helped develop the prototype for the service’s Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, for the 4th Infantry Division, using its proprietary AI-powered operating system Lattice.

“A common data layer allows the Army to integrate new systems without rebuilding the underlying architecture for every sensor, application, or weapon, so new capabilities can be fielded on the same foundation as those already in use,” Anduril said.

The Army awarded $162.8 million to Anduril to continue working on NGC2’s common data baseline, or software foundation, as it begins to implement it across the service’s I Corps, which commands service members across the Indo-Pacific.
The contract contains options that can grow its value up to $1.8 billion.
Anduril, along with Palantir, Raft and Striveworks, have helped build out the baseline.
The NGC2 system will allow technologies, weapons, sensors, devices and applications from across the force to operate on the same network and increase decision-making speed on the battlefield.

By expanding the NGC2 system to the I Corps, technologies will have to figure out ways to connect to the same network despite being separated by thousands of miles and experiencing interrupted or degraded connectivity.
This will provide the Army and Anduril an opportunity to test how well information flows between the systems as they access the NGC2 framework in a myriad of environments.

During a July 2026 ten-day event at Fort Irwin, California, entitled Project Convergence-Capstone 6 , the Army asked 10,000 participants from U.S. and allied forces, as well as industry partners using 90 technologies to test software for the NGC2.
Afterward, the Army awarded a contract to Anduril to develop the software prototype for NGC2 for the 4th Infantry Division.
Over the past year, Anduril has conducted several operational exercises in collaboration with the Army to test the NGC2’s common data layer baseline.

items.originalTitle: US Army to stand up command for unmanned and autonomous warfare
items.summary: The U.S. Army has ordered the creation of its own command for autonomous systems, a day after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a new four-star military command for unmanned and autonomous warfare. An Oct. 1 memo signed by Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle directs the Army vice chief of staff to establish the U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM. It also tells the assistant secretary of the Army for acquisition, logistics and technology, who oversees how the Army buys weapons, to put one office in charge of purchasing its priority autonomous systems.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army has ordered the creation of its own command for autonomous systems, a day after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a new four-star military command for unmanned and autonomous warfare.
An Oct. 1 memo signed by Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle directs the Army vice chief of staff to establish the U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM.

It also tells the assistant secretary of the Army for acquisition, logistics and technology, who oversees how the Army buys weapons, to put one office in charge of purchasing its priority autonomous systems.
Telle wrote that he issued the memo under guidance from Hegseth’s Sept. 30 State of the Force address .
The memo does not say who will lead FASCOM, where it will be based or when it will be established.
“Specifics on structure, command, mission, etc. will be announced at a future date,” Col.
Marty Meiners, an Army spokesperson, told Defense News.
The new acquisition office, a Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Autonomy, would have single authority over buying the Army’s priority autonomous systems.

“We are forging the U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command to get cutting-edge technology into the hands of soldiers, while prioritizing autonomy in our formations, our acquisitions, and our training to dominate the future of warfare.” Hegseth announced the Autonomous Warfare Command, or AutoWarCom, during his Sept. 30 State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia, Military Times reported .

Hegseth’s own memo, “ Project Agincourt: Pathway to the Autonomous Warfare Command ,” signed the same day as his address, puts the Pentagon’s unmanned systems office in charge of Project Agincourt, an effort to lay the groundwork for AutoWarCom.

As the Department of Defense eyes greater operability in the far north, these low temperatures can wreak havoc on equipment and machinery (and toilets), with ice becoming enemy No. 1.

evidenceRecords.text: Despite massive technological shifts, that paradigm still holds, which is why the U.S. Army and Navy have teamed up to keep systems operational — even in the extreme cold of the Arctic .

The team focused on different configurations of thermal wrappings, insulation and other components to ensure that parts of the kit’s components that are particularly vulnerable to cracking and freezing — hoses, valves, bladders and pumps — were able to withstand the greater threshold for cold, according to a recent Army release.

“Our armed forces live and operate in extremely cold and difficult conditions, so having these facilities operational is important for their physical and mental health while serving in the Arctic and other high-north environments,” said Dr. Dan Tague, a research chemist at CRREL, one of seven U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center laboratories.
Despite massive technological shifts, that paradigm still holds, which is why the U.S. Army and Navy have teamed up to keep systems operational — even in the extreme cold of the Arctic.
As the Department of Defense eyes greater operability in the far north, these low temperatures can wreak havoc on equipment and machinery (and toilets), with ice becoming enemy No. 1.

Which is why the Naval Facilities Engineering and Expeditionary Warfare Center, or NAVFAC EXWC, and the Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory, or CRREL, began working with both branches to field a rapidly deployable Triple Container rigid-wall shelter system usable in temperatures as low as -50 degrees Fahrenheit.
The already fielded version can operate in temperatures as low as -15 degrees Fahrenheit.
The result, per the release, far exceeded the objectives, with the TRICON-based system staying operational down to -65 degrees Fahrenheit.
Testing took place in CRREL’s New Hampshire-based Extreme Cold Chamber, a 288-square-foot cold room capable of reaching temperatures as low as -90 degrees Fahrenheit, per the release.

While military units typically have to wait until the Alaskan winter reaches its peak to simulate similar conditions, the controlled environment allowed the research team to create conditions similar to those of the real world.

items.summary: Nearly all U.S. soldiers completed a mandatory test meant to track the effects of blast exposure and monitor brain health across the Army, the service said in a release . The test, or Neurocognitive Assessment Tool, is computer-based and records neurological activity, such as attention, concentration, reaction time, memory, processing speed and decision-making. Testing started in 2024 in response to reports about the effects that routine weapons training can have on the brain, including traumatic brain injury.

evidenceRecords.text: Nearly all U.S. soldiers completed a mandatory test meant to track the effects of blast exposure and monitor brain health across the Army, the service said in a release .
The test, or Neurocognitive Assessment Tool, is computer-based and records neurological activity, such as attention, concentration, reaction time, memory, processing speed and decision-making.
Testing started in 2024 in response to reports about the effects that routine weapons training can have on the brain, including traumatic brain injury.

Active-duty, National Guard and Reserve soldiers in high-risk military occupational specialties, including combat engineers and explosive ordnance technicians, as well as troops operating heavy weapons systems, must take the assessment every year, starting soon after they enlist.
All other soldiers are required to test every three years.
Medical professionals use the data to monitor service members’ cognitive health throughout their military careers, allowing them to spot significant changes, including potential brain injuries.

“[The NCAT] is an important part of taking care of soldiers, but what this does is, it sets a baseline for reaction times and for memory,” Jordan Gillis, assistant secretary of the Army for installations, energy and environment, said in a release.

“By establishing a baseline for all soldiers, we’re able to monitor brain health, as well as … let medical providers help with treatment, if required.” According to the Sept. 30 release, the Army is expected to publish a directive about the Neurocognitive Assessment Tool and a broader overpressure program, which includes hazard assessment, exposure tracking, risk mitigation, cognitive monitoring, information management, illness and injury reporting and training and education.
“The takeaway is we are trying to take care of soldiers and monitor their health,” Gillis said.

“And if there is an impact, we’ll be able to treat them.” Reaching the milestone of 97% of soldiers being tested on the NCAT “demonstrates our commitment to cognitive safety, medical readiness and warfighting capability,” Gillis added.

The announcement of the milestone came just one month after the Government Accountability Office released the findings of its investigation into the ability of military services to provide the baseline cognitive assessments.

EDT Tuesday aboard a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, carrying more than 6,300 pounds of supplies and hardware, bound for the International Space Station.

Following its successful launch, the SpaceX Dragon spacecraft will carry new scientific experiments, cargo, and the final pair of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays to the orbiting laboratory.
Dragon is scheduled to autonomously dock at 11 a.m., Thursday, Oct. 15, to the space-facing port of the space station’s Harmony module.

Learn where to watch online: https://www.nasa.gov/live The final pair of solar arrays will complete the space station’s power system augmentation, boosting available electricity for research, operations, and the station’s safe, controlled deorbit.

Dragon also is delivering several new experiments, including hardware to manufacture artificial retinas in microgravity that could help restore vision for patients on Earth and 3D heart tissue models to advance large-scale drug testing on future space missions.

Dragon also will carry materials to study how a new type of glass is formed in microgravity, and brain organoids that could uncover potential treatment targets for neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and multiple sclerosis.
These are just a sample of the hundreds of investigations conducted aboard the orbiting laboratory in the areas of biology and biotechnology, physical sciences, and Earth and space science.
Research and technology investigations taking place aboard the space station benefit people on Earth and lay the groundwork for other agency deep space missions.

As part of NASA’s Artemis program, the agency will send astronauts to the Moon to prepare for future human exploration of Mars, inspiring the world through discovery in a new Golden Age of innovation and exploration.

items.title: How artificial neural networks build their own learning machinery
items.originalTitle: How artificial neural networks build their own learning machinery
items.summary: Artificial neural networks can learn to recognize images, use language, or write computer code. Like the brain’s circuits, they reorganize themselves as they learn, adjusting the strengths of their connections to improve their performance. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center argue that a crucial metric for the biological plausibility of an artificial neural network’s approach to learning is the network’s ability to organize itself, without the guiding hand of a developer.

evidenceRecords.text: Artificial neural networks can learn to recognize images, use language, or write computer code.
Like the brain’s circuits, they reorganize themselves as they learn, adjusting the strengths of their connections to improve their performance.

Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center argue that a crucial metric for the biological plausibility of an artificial neural network’s approach to learning is the network’s ability to organize itself, without the guiding hand of a developer.
They show that it is possible for an artificial neural network to build its own learning machinery.

“That’s not achievable by just designing a circuit that works very well.” An artificial neural network’s value to neuroscience should instead be judged by the extent to which it can organize itself — not just its connections, but also the machinery that adjusts those connections.

“If the synaptic motifs we propose are, in fact, used by the brain to do what backpropagation does for artificial neural networks, then we will have a strong connection at the level of fundamental mechanisms between artificial and natural networks — between machines and brains,” he says.

Engineers and technicians on Aug. 31, 2026, used a crane to position the spacecraft within the towering chamber, where Griffin-1 alternately baked at up to 167 degrees Fahrenheit (75 degrees Celsius) and froze at temperatures as low as minus 148 F (minus 100 C).
Figure A In Figure A, engineers and technicians move Griffin-1 through a hallway leading to the 25-Foot Space Simulator on Aug. 31.

Figure B Figure B shows Griffin-1 on July 29 in an anechoic chamber for electromagnetic interference and electromagnetic compatibility testing, which ensures signals from the spacecraft’s electronic components don’t interfere with one another.

Figure C In Figure C, taken on July 20, Griffin-1 rotates rapidly on a special table to measure its mass properties, enabling engineers to look for any unexpected wobbles as they assess how the vehicle will move through space — vital information for determining the spacecraft’s readiness for flight and surface operations.

Figure D In Figure D, microphones are arrayed around Griffin-1 on Aug. 12 during acoustic testing in which giant horns powered by compressed gaseous nitrogen blast the spacecraft with up to 153 decibels inside the sealed acoustic chamber to mimic the roar of launch.

Griffin-1 also endured vibration testing, during which hundreds of sensors monitored the spacecraft as a “shaker table” rattled it in three directions — with increasingly intense force — to simulate the ride out of Earth’s atmosphere atop a rocket.
After proving its mettle at JPL, Griffin-1 was shipped back across the country to Voyager Lunar Systems’ Pittsburgh facility for final assembly.
Part of NASA’s CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) initiative within the Moon Base Program, Griffin-1 is expected to launch in late 2026 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket.

items.title: The Lynx XM30 is making its case to be the US Army’s Bradley replacement
items.originalTitle: The Lynx XM30 is making its case to be the US Army’s Bradley replacement
items.summary: American Rheinmetall , one of two defense companies chosen to develop replacements for the Army’s M2 Bradley Fighting Vehicle , announced in September the delivery of its Lynx XM30 prototype to the service. The Army conducted initial safety tests before allowing soldiers to join the trial-and-error phase. “Now it’s in soldiers’ hands,” said Chris Haag, vice president of business development and strategy at Rheinmetall.

evidenceRecords.text: American Rheinmetall , one of two defense companies chosen to develop replacements for the Army’s M2 Bradley Fighting Vehicle , announced in September the delivery of its Lynx XM30 prototype to the service.
The Army conducted initial safety tests before allowing soldiers to join the trial-and-error phase.
“Now it’s in soldiers’ hands,” said Chris Haag, vice president of business development and strategy at Rheinmetall.

“Seeing their eyes light up when they got to see the vehicle for the first time is pretty awesome.” While Haag could not disclose where soldiers were along the tinkering process, he confirmed that service members were in possession of the vehicle and were at least able to hop inside and turn it on, beginning a new era for Army combat vehicles.

Rheinmetall is currently competing for the XM30 Army contract with General Dynamics Land Systems, which is unveiling its Wolf XM30 prototype at the Association of the U.S. Army Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., from Oct. 12 to 14.
The Army selected the companies in 2023 for the design phase of a process that will eventually replace the Bradley, which arrived in the 1980s.
The Lynx XM30 is designed for modern combat environments riddled with drones and electronic warfare, like those seen in Ukraine.
The vehicle will wield a hybrid-electric powertrain and an uncrewed 50mm turret, providing more firepower than the Bradley, which boasts a 25mm M242 Bushmaster.

American Rheinmetall’s prototype likely wouldn’t differ from General Dynamics’ XM30 design when it came to physical architecture, Haag said, which meant the Lynx could differentiate itself from competition through aspects like power, engine, transmission and soldiers’ experience with user interface and operability in general.

For large modernization efforts, the M2 Bradley Fighting Vehicle may have to travel back to an Army or manufacturing facility to undergo overhauls or block upgrades, whereas the XM30 could potentially undergo software updates that revamp the system in a much shorter timeframe and require less geographical displacement.

The company will deliver seven more prototypes to the Army by the end of the year, all part of a nearly $764 million Engineering and Manufacturing Development contract to expand the XM30 from digital design through validation.

evidenceRecords.text: CASA said respondents broadly supported the objectives of the three proposals, covering a risk-based approach to determine when a NOTAM is required for an area approval, relocating existing record keeping and information requirements, and nationally consistent remote pilot licence examinations.
Feedback highlighted the need for clear and consistent NOTAM decision making and practical implementation arrangements.
Respondents considered that this could reduce briefing workload and information overload, helping airspace users identify operationally important information.
Submissions also emphasised the importance of maintaining aviation safety.
Examples included emergency services, military activity, aerial work, mustering and other general aviation operations.
Some submissions indicated a preference for NOTAM publication to remain the default, or to continue for all drone and rocket operations.
Respondents consistently emphasised the need for clear and nationally consistent criteria for determining when a NOTAM is required.

Suggested factors included operating height and duration, proximity to aerodromes and flight paths, airspace classification, the likelihood of low-level crewed aircraft, the dimensions of the approved area and other available risk controls.
Some respondents also sought greater clarity about how NOTAM decisions would be documented and communicated.
Suggestions included recording whether a NOTAM is required in the area approval and maintaining a record of the basis for the decision.
Feedback also noted that unclear criteria could lead operators to submit precautionary NOTAM requests, potentially limiting the intended benefits of the proposal.
Respondents sought clarity about who would request or arrange NOTAM publication, applicable lead times, and how changes, cancellations and system outages would be managed.

items.title: Launch preview: NASA, SpaceX to launch new solar arrays, 6,300 pounds of cargo to the space station
items.originalTitle: Launch preview: NASA, SpaceX to launch new solar arrays, 6,300 pounds of cargo to the space station
items.summary: SpaceX and NASA are preparing to fly a resupply cargo flight to the International Space Station on Tuesday morning. The pre-sunrise launch will be SpaceX’s 35th mission to the orbiting outpost as part of NASA’s Commercial Resupply Services (CRS) contract. Liftoff of SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station is scheduled for 6:33 a.m. Stowed in the unpressurized trunk of Dragon C211 is the final pair of ISS Roll-Out Solar Arrays (iROSAs), which will help to augment the power generation of the aging space station.

items.originalTitle: Bloq Quantum Launches Bloq Maya AI Agent for Enterprise Quantum Computing
items.summary: Insider Brief Bloq Quantum has launched Bloq Maya, an AI agent designed to help enterprise quantum teams develop, test, and implement quantum computing use cases. The platform offers more than 15 pre-built algorithms, a visual quantum circuit builder, an experiments module, and execution across cloud simulators and quantum hardware providers. Bloq Quantum says Bloq Maya can help teams develop quantum use cases up to 10 times faster, targeting applications such as financial risk modeling, portfolio optimization, and complex simulations.

PRESS RELEASE — Bloq Quantum today announced the launch of Bloq Maya, its flagship AI Agent designed to simplify and accelerate quantum computing for enterprises.
It’s built to solve a very specific problem: making quantum computing actually usable for enterprise quantum teams.
The launch of Bloq Maya addresses a critical bottleneck in the industry: translating complex theoretical quantum concepts into production-ready business solutions.
Bloq Maya functions as an intelligent AI partner.
Through a simple conversational interface, you can ask Maya to generate custom quantum circuits, build QUBOs, review algorithms, or generate optimized quantum code.
“Translating complex quantum workflows into production-ready enterprise applications remains a massive bottleneck for enterprises,” said Sreekuttan L S, Co-Founder and CEO of Bloq Quantum.

“Bloq Maya removes the friction so teams can go from an idea to a tested quantum use case up to 10x faster.” The platform integrates this agentic AI seamlessly into Bloq ‘s unified workspace, offering several key features: Low-Code Algorithm Library: Access to over 15 pre-built, advanced research-grade algorithms, including QKAN, PQK, QEMCMC, and QSVM.
Visual Circuit Studio: An intuitive visual builder for designing parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs), feature maps, and complex gate compositions without deep quantum coding.
Experiments Module: A streamlined environment for testing use cases against quantum algorithms.

The company will continue bringing its ElliQ AI companion to aging New Yorkers at risk of loneliness and social isolation.
With the expansion, NYSOFA and Intuition Robotics created a new three-year, $2.1 million agreement.
The expansion builds on the organizations’ three years of experience working together.
During that time, ElliQ has demonstrated its ability to reduce loneliness and improve health and wellbeing.
The robot also helps older adults remain healthier and more independent in their own homes.

“Loneliness and isolation are commonly heard today, but make no mistake, the health effects are devastating, and NYSOFA is working continuously to provide the help older New Yorkers need,” said Greg Olsen, director of the office .

“ElliQ is an essential tool to help combat the loneliness epidemic, joining dozens of other projects launched by NYSOFA to overcome the digital divide, address social isolation, improve health and wellness, and support caregivers.” NYSOFA established its first public-private partnership in 2018, following a report by AARP and the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) on the impact of loneliness and social isolation on older adults and Medicare spending.
It stated that loneliness and isolation are equivalent to smoking almost a pack of cigarettes per day, cost Medicare more than $7 billion to treat, and make chronic conditions worse.
In addition to its partnership with NYSOFA, Intuition Robotics has similar partnerships in Wisconsin, Florida, and Washington.
In Washington, the program is aimed at Medicaid recipients .

“This partnership extension continues our long term partnership with the state of New York, and its Office for the Aging, reflecting three years of measurable, record-breaking engagement results: older adults across New York are engaging with ElliQ more often, feeling less lonely, and staying more connected to the people who matter to them,” said Dor Skuler, co-founder and CEO of Intuition Robotics.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Quantum XChange CEO Eddy Zervigon will moderate a panel on post-quantum cryptography implementation at the ACT-IAC 2026 Cyber Summit on October 14 in Reston, Virginia.

The discussion will cover crypto-agility, encryption lifecycle management, quantum-safe network deployment, and the risk of “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks across enterprise and government systems.
The panel follows Quantum XChange ’s reported deployment of its Phio TX-EM solution at a federal agency and the company’s recent partnerships to expand access to its quantum-safe security products.

PRESS RELEASE — Quantum XChange ® , a leader in quantum-safe network security, today announced that CEO Eddy Zervigon will moderate a panel discussion on post-quantum cryptography at the ACT-IAC 2026 Cyber Summit on October 14 in Reston, Virginia.
The discussion will focus on the practical challenges of implementing post-quantum cryptography (PQC) across enterprise and government networks.

The panel, titled “ Implementing Enterprise Security for Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) ,” comes just days after the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) released a report highlighting challenges federal agencies face in preparing for the transition to post-quantum cryptography.

The discussion will examine real-world implementation challenges, lessons learned, and best practices for managing encryption lifecycles, achieving crypto-agility, and deploying quantum-safe security across complex enterprise environments.
The panel will also address the growing threat of “Harvest Now, Decrypt Later” attacks, in which adversaries collect encrypted data today for potential decryption by future quantum computers.
“Transitioning to post-quantum cryptography is a complex undertaking, particularly across large government networks with critical systems and infrastructure,” said Zervigon.
Quantum XChange recently helped a federal agency deploy quantum-safe security across its production sites using existing network infrastructure.

This panel is an opportunity to bring government and industry leaders together to share practical experiences, lessons learned, and approaches that can help accelerate that transition.” The federal deployment , announced October 8, used Quantum XChange ’s Phio TX-EM ® solution to add post-quantum protection without requiring major hardware replacement.

items.title: Google Researchers Propose Using Error Records to Improve Quantum Results After Computation
items.originalTitle: Google Researchers Propose Using Error Records to Improve Quantum Results After Computation
items.summary: Insider Brief Google Quantum AI researchers developed a method that uses saved error-correction records to reduce distortion in quantum results after a calculation, achieving more than 1,000-fold suppression in simulations. The method compares a fast decoder with a more accurate offline decoder and adjusts how much each measurement counts toward the answer, avoiding separate calibration experiments or changes to quantum circuits.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Google Quantum AI researchers developed a method that uses saved error-correction records to reduce distortion in quantum results after a calculation, achieving more than 1,000-fold suppression in simulations.

The method compares a fast decoder with a more accurate offline decoder and adjusts how much each measurement counts toward the answer, avoiding separate calibration experiments or changes to quantum circuits.
The results rely on simplified noise simulations, and the method requires additional measurements and further testing under realistic conditions and on quantum hardware.
Errors can survive even a quantum computer’s built-in correction system, leaving researchers with results that look reliable but remain slightly off.

Now, Google Quantum AI researchers report on a “measure now, mitigate later” approach in a preprint study on arXiv that uses error records saved during the calculation as a way to reduce that remaining distortion by more than 1,000-fold in simulations.
Their method, called virtual error cancellation, moves part of the work to a conventional computer after the quantum calculation ends.
It uses information the quantum system already collects to adjust how individual measurement results contribute to the final answer.
According to the study, the approach avoids separate experiments to measure noise and does not require changes to the quantum circuits running the calculation.
Researchers must repeat measurements to produce a precise answer, and the gains have yet to be demonstrated on quantum hardware.
The findings point to a possible way to get more accurate estimates from early fault-tolerant quantum computers.

The collaboration combines SQOUT’s threat intelligence and risk assessment tools with TTP’s laboratory testing to identify and evaluate vulnerabilities in quantum key distribution systems. PRESS RELEASE — QuDef, a Netherlands-based leader in quantum technology security, and The Thought Projects (TTP), a Singapore-based innovation leader in future-proof data security and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) security evaluation, today announced a strategic collaboration.
The two companies have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) under which TTP will bring QuDef’s flagship SQOUT ® platform to Singapore and the broader Asia-Pacific market.
The collaboration aims to strengthen the security assurance ecosystem for quantum communication technologies and support the adoption of trusted quantum-safe solutions across the region.

As governments, critical infrastructure operators, telecommunications providers, and enterprises deploy QKD alongside post-quantum cryptography (PQC), the security of the deployed systems, not only of the underlying protocols, has become a strategic priority.

Bringing European quantum security expertise to Asia-Pacific SQOUT ® is QuDef’s threat intelligence and knowledge platform which is used for systematic threat and risk assessment of QKD products and quantum communication networks.

items.title: US Army suspends longtime hometown recruiter assistance program, faces cancellation
items.originalTitle: US Army suspends longtime hometown recruiter assistance program, faces cancellation
items.summary: The service’s decades-old Hometown Recruiter Assistance Program has been suspended, Lt. Gen. Johnny Davis confirmed at a forum hosted by the Association of the United States Army. “I would tell you, when the program was initiated and really delivered to the Army years ago and executed, that we had some good return on investment — about, you know, one or two percent,” Davis said in response to a question at the forum.

evidenceRecords.text: The service’s decades-old Hometown Recruiter Assistance Program has been suspended, Lt.
Army recruiting social media pages began discussing the suspension of the Hometown Recruiter Assistance Program in January, though the service has not publicly addressed the move until now.
The service’s decades-old Hometown Recruiter Assistance Program has been suspended, Lt. Gen. Johnny Davis confirmed at a forum hosted by the Association of the United States Army.

“I would tell you, when the program was initiated and really delivered to the Army years ago and executed, that we had some good return on investment — about, you know, one or two percent,” Davis said in response to a question at the forum.
Davis said leaders understood the “human element” of what was happening, in that new graduates were eager to reconnect with family and friends in what amounted to additional uncharged leave.
But, he added, the Army had to consider what it was getting out of the arrangement.

Likewise, he said, the Army has in the past allowed National Guard and Reserve soldiers to return home for non-charged leave during the holiday break known as the Christmas Exodus on the understanding that they would support Army recruiting as ambassadors during that time.
“During that Christmas holiday, was there a lot of recruiters in the recruiting stations working with them?
No,” Davis said. “So we’re really thinking through: is this return on investment, and is it worth the cost to the Army?
Or can we take those funds and spend them in other ways to help our men and women.”
Davis said leaders were now “looking at other ways” to help soldiers get coveted hometown leave apart from the hometown recruiting program.
In a 2022 Army news release, a recruiting center station commander in Missouri, Staff Sgt.
Colton Dunbar, said the success of the program came down to “how the soldiers are leveraged.”

items.title: Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
items.originalTitle: Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
items.summary: A key energy facility supplying Kyiv with heating and electricity has been hit in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Darnytska CHP-4, or CHPP-4, and a residential building were hit in a strike the president said came with "no early warning from our partners". Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said one person was killed and 13 injured in the missile strike on the apartment block late on Tuesday. Four people were in a serious condition, he said.

evidenceRecords.text: A key energy facility supplying Kyiv with heating and electricity has been hit in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
Darnytska CHP-4, or CHPP-4, and a residential building were hit in a strike the president said came with "no early warning from our partners".
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said one person was killed and 13 injured in the missile strike on the apartment block late on Tuesday.
Four people were in a serious condition, he said.
It comes two days after US President Donald Trump said an energy ceasefire had been agreed by Russia and Ukraine, although Kyiv reported multiple Russian strikes following the announcement.
"Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire.
Russia is targeting yet another power plant and the lives of our people," Zelensky said on social media following Tuesday's strikes.
"This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added.
It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles.
Following strikes on Monday night, there was speculation America had cut off access to key intelligence enabling Ukraine to track incoming threats.
Asked about Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites, Trump said: "Ukraine hit many sites the day before."

items.title: Agentic AI Automates RTL Waveform Analysis And Debugging (Columbia, Google)
items.originalTitle: Agentic AI Automates RTL Waveform Analysis And Debugging (Columbia, Google)
items.summary: Researchers at Columbia University, Google DeepMind, and Google published a technical paper titled “Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification.” Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have made rapid inroads into Electronic Design Automation (EDA), approximately 74.6% of existing studies target static Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging largely untouched.

evidenceRecords.text: Researchers at Columbia University, Google DeepMind , and Google published a technical paper titled “Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification.” Abstract “The unprecedented computational scale of modern artificial intelligence depends on complex, multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip, yet the workflows that verify these chips remain stubbornly manual.

Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have made rapid inroads into Electronic Design Automation (EDA), approximately 74.6% of existing studies target static Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging largely untouched.

BTTF distills massive, unstructured simulation dumps into a normalized relational SQLite database and couples it with a collaborative multi-agent orchestration engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL while correlating signal anomalies with versioned RTL repositories.
Across a 150-query benchmark, BTTF attains 95.33% execution accuracy, charting a practical path toward autonomous EDA verification.” Find the technical paper here .

items.title: All Systems Go: Global PC App Ecosystem Ready for NVIDIA RTX Spark
items.originalTitle: All Systems Go: Global PC App Ecosystem Ready for NVIDIA RTX Spark
items.summary: NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip. With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and CUDA technologies for creators, developers and gamers, while unlocking a new paradigm in personal computing via powerful local AI agents. Last week, NVIDIA and Microsoft announced that RTX Spark laptops will be available on Friday, Oct. 16 .

evidenceRecords.text: NVIDIA RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — a reinvention combining the capabilities of a gaming PC, a creative studio and a personal AI supercomputer into a single superchip.

With up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute, RTX Spark delivers the full stack of NVIDIA RTX and CUDA technologies for creators, developers and gamers, while unlocking a new paradigm in personal computing via powerful local AI agents.
Last week, NVIDIA and Microsoft announced that RTX Spark laptops will be available on Friday, Oct. 16 .
Ahead of the launch, NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners are rolling out new software features and performance optimizations to expand what’s possible with local AI on RTX Spark.
The NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B model, purpose-built for agentic AI on RTX Spark, releases on Thursday, Oct. 15.
Developer tools are now ready for RTX Spark: Top developer frameworks are now available for RTX Spark, including PyTorch, Python and CUDA, as well as all CUDA libraries.

Hundreds of top games and anti-cheat are supported on RTX Spark, plus: A 2x faster DLSS 5 AI model arrives Friday, Oct. 16, and a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation is available today via the NVIDIA App beta .
From models to agent harnesses to security to tools, NVIDIA is partnering closely with the local AI ecosystem to make RTX Spark the ideal hardware to run local agents.
Local AI Agents Made Easy On RTX Spark From the first boot of RTX Spark, users will be greeted with a “Getting Started” screen to choose and install their agent app.
These agents will come with new, secure sandboxing technology thanks to NVIDIA OpenShell and MXC.
The apps will recommend an optimized local model and settings configuration for RTX Spark, and set it all up for users in a few clicks.
NVIDIA has also now made available MCPs for its applications, including NVIDIA App, Broadcast, PAIR, Omniverse, RTX Remix and a large library of CUDA-X Skills .

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Infleqtion has received £9 million from Innovate UK to develop Quantum Spectrum-DF, a deployable quantum radio frequency direction-finding system under the second phase of the QuDiFi project.

PRESS RELEASE — Infleqtion (NYSE: INFQ), a global leader in quantum computing and quantum sensing powered by neutral-atom technology, has been awarded £9 million (~$12M) by Innovate UK, part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), to continue development of a deployable quantum radio frequency (QRF) direction finding (DF) system as part of the Quantum Missions Primer programme.

“By advancing quantum sensing from laboratory research to practical deployment, this project will help establish the United Kingdom as a leader in next generation radio frequency sensing technologies,” said Colin Sullivan, Managing Director, UK at Infleqtion .
For more information about Infleqtion ’s sensing capabilities, visit: Quantum Spectrum Sensing | Infleqtion .
Infleqtion has received £9 million from Innovate UK to develop Quantum Spectrum-DF, a deployable quantum radio frequency direction-finding system under the second phase of the QuDiFi project.
Developed in collaboration with Leonardo, the technology is intended for defence and civilian applications, including spectrum monitoring, passive radar, and resilient navigation.

Infleqtion is developing a Quantum Spectrum-DF product within the second phase of the Quantum Direction Finding (QuDiFi) project, designed to accurately detect and locate signals in environments where existing technologies are limited.

“By advancing quantum sensing from laboratory research to practical deployment, this project will help establish the United Kingdom as a leader in next generation radio frequency sensing technologies,” said Colin Sullivan, Managing Director, UK at Infleqtion. “The technology also lays the groundwork for future applications such as spectrum surveillance, passive radar and resilient navigation, enabling new capabilities that are not achievable with existing systems.”
Radio signals are essential to modern communications, navigation, and monitoring systems.
The ability to determine where these signals originate is critical for applications ranging from defence and security to emergency response and protection of infrastructure.
However, current direction-finding systems often rely on large antenna arrays, especially at lower frequencies, which limits their use in mobile and space-constrained environments.
For more information about Infleqtion’s sensing capabilities, visit: Quantum Spectrum Sensing | Infleqtion.

“By advancing quantum sensing from laboratory research to practical deployment, this project will help establish the United Kingdom as a leader in next generation radio frequency sensing technologies,” said Colin Sullivan, Managing Director, UK at Infleqtion.
