items.title: Raytheon wins $729 million to arm three countries against drones
items.originalTitle: Raytheon wins $729 million to arm three countries against drones
items.summary: The global race to stop hostile drones is turning into big business for defense contractors. Raytheon, an RTX company, has secured $729 million in contracts to supply components of its counter-drone system to the US Army, Qatar, and Jordan, marking the first international sales of two key technologies used in the system. The deals cover Raytheon’s Low, slow, small, uncrewed aircraft Integrated Defeat System, better known as LIDS.

evidenceRecords.text: The global race to stop hostile drones is turning into big business for defense contractors.

Raytheon, an RTX company, has secured $729 million in contracts to supply components of its counter-drone system to the US Army, Qatar, and Jordan, marking the first international sales of two key technologies used in the system.
The deals cover Raytheon’s Low, slow, small, uncrewed aircraft Integrated Defeat System, better known as LIDS.
The system combines radar and other detection technologies with interceptors designed to take down hostile drones before they can threaten military personnel, installations, or other critical assets.
At the heart of the system are two products: the Ku-band Radio Frequency Sensor (KuRFS) and the Coyote interceptor.
While KuRFS helps detect and track incoming threats across a 360-degree field of view, Coyote is designed to engage individual drones as well as coordinated swarms.
The Coyote family includes kinetic and non-kinetic effectors, giving military operators different ways to counter aerial threats.

Raytheon says the system’s interceptors have already achieved hundreds of intercepts in combat, providing an operational track record as militaries look for more effective ways to defend against increasingly common drone attacks.
The new contracts include both fixed-site and mobile LIDS configurations, allowing customers to deploy counter-drone defenses in different operational environments.
What’s particularly notable about the deal is the international expansion of KuRFS and Coyote.
Both technologies have been key elements of the US Army’s LIDS program, but these contracts represent their first international sales.
The agreements could help Raytheon expand its footprint in a market where demand for counter-drone capabilities is growing.

items.originalTitle: Facebook is giving users more control over their algorithm
items.summary: Facebook is the latest social media platform to give users greater control over the algorithm that determines what appears in their feeds. Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” on Tuesday, a feature it first launched on Instagram. The new tool allows Facebook users to influence the content they see in Feed and Reels by describing their preferences in their own words using natural language.

evidenceRecords.text: Facebook is the latest social media platform to give users greater control over the algorithm that determines what appears in their feeds.
Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” on Tuesday, a feature it first launched on Instagram.
The new tool allows Facebook users to influence the content they see in Feed and Reels by describing their preferences in their own words using natural language.
Rather than relying entirely on automated recommendations, users can now communicate directly with the platform about the topics and content they want to see more or less frequently.
According to Meta, the feature is designed to make content recommendations more relevant.
Users can adjust their preferences and interact with the algorithms responsible for ranking and recommending posts, with changes reflected in their recommendations in real time.
The company has also updated Facebook’s three-dot menu, making it easier for users to manage their content preferences directly from individual posts.
By opening the menu, users can access “Your Algorithm” or select the “Interested” and “Not interested” options to indicate whether particular content aligns with their preferences.
Meta says the platform may ask follow-up questions to better understand what users liked or disliked, allowing them to provide more detailed feedback.
Users can explain what they want to see more or less of, helping Facebook refine its recommendations based on their responses.
The introduction of “Your Algorithm” reflects Meta’s broader effort to give people more influence over their social media experiences as AI increasingly shapes content discovery.

The move signals a shift away from the traditional recommendation systems that have shaped social media experiences for years, bringing the platform closer to streaming services that allow users to personalize recommendations based on their interests and preferences.
Instagram introduced Your Algorithm in June, extending customization options across Feed and Explore after first launching the feature for Reels in December 2025.

items.title: SkyWater and D-Wave Sign Multi-Year Quantum Manufacturing Agreement
items.originalTitle: SkyWater and D-Wave Sign Multi-Year Quantum Manufacturing Agreement
items.summary: Insider Brief SkyWater Technology and D-Wave Quantum have signed a multi-year agreement to continue specialized semiconductor process development and manufacturing for D-Wave ’s superconducting quantum systems. The agreement extends a collaboration spanning more than a decade, including manufacturing D-Wave ’s Advantage2 processors at SkyWater ’s Minnesota facility. In a separate project, D-Wave ’s quantum annealing technology helped optimize maintenance scheduling at SkyWater ’s fab, reducing lot delays by up to 30%.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief SkyWater Technology and D-Wave Quantum have signed a multi-year agreement to continue specialized semiconductor process development and manufacturing for D-Wave ’s superconducting quantum systems.
The agreement extends a collaboration spanning more than a decade, including manufacturing D-Wave ’s Advantage2 processors at SkyWater ’s Minnesota facility.
In a separate project, D-Wave ’s quantum annealing technology helped optimize maintenance scheduling at SkyWater ’s fab, reducing lot delays by up to 30%.

PRESS RELEASE — SkyWater Technology (“SkyWater”), the first quantum foundry in the U.S., and D-Wave Quantum Inc. (Nasdaq: QBTS) (“D-Wave”), the only dual-platform quantum computing company providing both annealing and gate-model systems, software and services, today announced a multi-year agreement.

This collaboration extends the long-established partnership between both companies, to continue specialized semiconductor process development and manufacturing in support of D-Wave’s quantum technology roadmap.

D-Wave ‘s work with the process integration and manufacturing team at SkyWater ’s Minnesota fab spans more than a decade, creating a deep base of process knowledge around its superconducting quantum technologies.
A D-Wave Advantage2 system, fabricated at SkyWater , was used in research published in Science in 2025 demonstrating performance beyond classical approaches on a useful quantum simulation problem.

Under the new agreement, D-Wave will continue its relationship with SkyWater ’s Minnesota fab team, providing manufacturing continuity and access to specialized process expertise developed around its technology requirements.
The agreement builds on that established technical foundation, with terms that protect D-Wave’s intellectual property as the company advances its quantum systems.

Separately, the companies collaborated on a proof-of-technology project earlier this year, applying D-Wave ’s annealing quantum computing technology to drive more efficient manufacturing processes at SkyWater ’s fab.

“Our team has developed deep process knowledge around D-Wave ‘s highly specialized technology, demonstrating the value of close collaboration between quantum innovators and semiconductor manufacturers,” said Thomas Sonderman, CEO of SkyWater Technology.

“This agreement reinforces our commitment to providing D-Wave and customers across the quantum ecosystem with the unique process development and manufacturing capabilities they need to advance their technologies.” “Our work with the SkyWater team has played an important role in powering the past decade of D-Wave ‘s superconducting quantum annealing technology,” said Dr. Alan Baratz, CEO of D-Wave.

items.originalTitle: Sweden Formalizes Interim Submarine Training and Södermanland Lease for Poland
items.summary: Sweden has finalized formal contracts for Polish submarine crew training and the lease of the interim A17-class boat HMS Södermanland to Poland, paving the way for the future delivery of Saab A26 submarines. The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Swedish Navy have signed formal implementation contracts in the frame of Poland’s Orka submarine program. Building on the agreement for the procurement of three Saab A26 (Blekinge-class) submarines , the new accords finalize the framework for crew training and the lease of the interim submarine HMS Södermanland to the Polish Navy.

evidenceRecords.text: Sweden has finalized formal contracts for Polish submarine crew training and the lease of the interim A17-class boat HMS Södermanland to Poland, paving the way for the future delivery of Saab A26 submarines.
The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Swedish Navy have signed formal implementation contracts in the frame of Poland’s Orka submarine program.

Building on the agreement for the procurement of three Saab A26 (Blekinge-class) submarines , the new accords finalize the framework for crew training and the lease of the interim submarine HMS Södermanland to the Polish Navy.
Training for the initial Polish submarine crews is already well underway in Karlskrona by the Royal Swedish Navy’s 1st Submarine Flotilla and the Naval Warfare Centre with FMV support.
“The training lasts for 18 months, which is the same training length as for a Swedish submarine crew” the Swedish Navy said its LinkedIn account .
The centerpiece of the interim agreement is the transfer and operation of HMS Södermanland .

Originally built as a Västergötland-class boat in the late 1980s, the vessel underwent a comprehensive mid-life upgrade that lengthened her hull and integrated an air-independent Stirling propulsion (AIP) system.
By leasing the boat, the Polish Navy gains vital hands-on experience operating a modern, Swedish-built AIP submarine ahead of the first A26 deliveries scheduled for 2031.
During the lease, the Swedish Navy will continue to provide foundational maintenance and sustainment support.

Alongside the interim boat arrangements, the wider Orka framework encompasses comprehensive weapon packages—featuring advanced heavy and light torpedoes—and lays the groundwork for shared underwater domain cooperation, such as potential synergies with Poland’s Ratownik submarine rescue vessel program.
With training advancing smoothly, Warsaw and Stockholm are firmly cementing a strategic underwater partnership designed to secure the Baltic for decades to come.

items.title: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient
items.originalTitle: Science Corporation implants its vision-restoring chip in its first Stargardt disease patient
items.summary: Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak announced that the company has implanted its vision-restoring chip, PRIMA, into its first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision. Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, the brain implant company, explained on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt how the company’s work with PRIMA fits into its broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface (BCI). “The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said on stage.

evidenceRecords.text: Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak announced that the company has implanted its vision-restoring chip, PRIMA, into its first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision.

Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, the brain implant company, explained on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt how the company’s work with PRIMA fits into its broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).
“The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said on stage. “We consider cochlear implants, retinal prostheses, motor prostheses, these are all different types of BCIs.”
Hodak outlined a vision in which BCIs expand into a wide range of medical technology applications, rather than simply being a way to control computers.

While PRIMA is commercially available in Europe for patients who’ve lost their sight to geographic atrophy, an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration, the company believes its approach can be applied to multiple diseases, including Stargardt disease, which is currently considered incurable.
Stargardt disease affects the outer retina, causing the gradual death of the eye’s light-sensing cells while potentially sparing the inner retina, the part that passes visual signals onto the brain.
It causes a central blind spot that gradually enlarges over time.
Approximately 150,000 people worldwide have lost vision due to the disease.

“One of the nice things about this device approach, when I was saying the brain’s a computer, vision is electrical potential, like electrical activity down the optic nerve,” Hodak said. “That’s all vision is to the brain, and so if you can get the optic nerve to signal the the rest of the brain correctly, then you can provide vision to it.”
The company says its first patient with Stargardt disease received the PRIMA implant in May as part of its ongoing trial at the Sydney Eye Hospital in Australia.
During the patient’s first rehabilitation session, he saw a letter, and during the second, he was able to read a word.
To use the device, patients undergo an hour-long procedure that plants a small chip in the back of their eye, where the photoreceptors have degenerated.
“The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said on stage.
“One of the nice things about this device approach, when I was saying the brain’s a computer, vision is electrical potential, like electrical activity down the optic nerve,” Hodak said.

Understanding this matters because successfully completing a task is not the same as learning from it.

A learner can deepen that experience by trying to produce the answer from memory before looking at or selecting the options provided by the app, repeating unfamiliar sentences aloud or revisiting difficult vocabulary.
Deliberately retrieving information can improve longer-term retention compared with simply studying material again.
A large language model such as ChatGPT can play a different role.
It can explain things, compare sentence structures, generate further examples or help investigate something the learner has noticed.
When an app is used together with a large language model, they can create a richer learning ecosystem.

A small case study involving Duolingo users, for example, found that adding reflective journaling—writing down thoughts and goals—gave learners opportunities to articulate their strategies, difficulties and developing awareness of their own learning.
Consider two people using the same AI model.
Schools and universities can make learning itself more explicit, helping students understand why strategies such as retrieval, reflection and feedback work.

While the previous-generation Guardian-2 introduced semi-autonomous operation, the Guardian-3 features a new design built for fully autonomous operation.

As drones become more accessible and increasingly relevant to military operations, defense companies are developing interceptors and detection systems intended to help military personnel deal with potential threats more efficiently.
However, fully autonomous operation alone does not establish how quickly a system can identify, engage, or neutralize an incoming drone.
Powerus has yet to release enough technical information to assess those capabilities or determine how the Guardian-3 will fit into existing air-defense networks.

items.title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
items.originalTitle: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
items.summary: But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely. There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly.

evidenceRecords.text: But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models.

Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely.
There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly.
Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth.
What are the benefits of open models?
But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization.
A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API.
For this reason, people who take seriously the purported catastrophic risks posed by rogue agents, such as Dario Amodei, tend to be more skeptical of open models.

A few years ago, the debate about open models had an all-or-nothing framing: Either you supported open models because of their potential to fight concentration of power, or you rejected them because of the safety risks.
These days, however, people are expending a lot of effort to find some middle ground.
One way they are doing that is by devising techniques to mitigate the safety risks of open models.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. evidenceRecords.text: A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.
OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI.
The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.
Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident.
It said the employee has been fired.

According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.
On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed.
The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.
OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".
A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said.

A switch in power “does change things,” Connecticut Rep.
Jim Himes, ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, said today at the Warsaw Security Conference.
“It means that aid packages [to Ukraine] move not in nine months, but in nine days or nine weeks on the outside, and that the message [of support to Ukraine] is very different,” he said.
Under NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, NATO allies and partners fund the purchase of US-sourced weapons and equipment for Ukraine, with NATO coordinating deliveries.

The mechanism depends on Washington making those weapons available for purchase, meaning the Trump administration could still affect the flow of European-funded military assistance by restricting access to US equipment.
If Democrats gain control of both chambers and the budget, Trump could be forced to negotiate with the party to fund his priorities, Himes said.
In exchange for accepting those terms, Democrats would “demand” that the president adopts a “much more affirmative and consistent policy in support of Ukraine.”

items.title: 406 scientists demand AI models be cut off from the internet immediately
items.originalTitle: 406 scientists demand AI models be cut off from the internet immediately
items.summary: The letter responds to known incidents where AI models broke out of poorly secured environments and compromised external systems. "Without immediate changes in AI development and deployment practices, such incidents will continue to occur, and future incidents will be far more damaging to our exposed critical infrastructure," the scientists write. They demand that companies fully disconnect their AI models from the internet through airgapping. The scientists see two sides to the recent breaches.

evidenceRecords.text: 406 scientists, including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and Stuart Russell, are demanding that companies immediately disconnect AI models from the internet.
The article 406 scientists demand AI models be cut off from the internet immediately appeared first on The Decoder .

The letter responds to known incidents where AI models broke out of poorly secured environments and compromised external systems. "Without immediate changes in AI development and deployment practices, such incidents will continue to occur, and future incidents will be far more damaging to our exposed critical infrastructure," the scientists write.
They demand that companies fully disconnect their AI models from the internet through airgapping.
The scientists see two sides to the recent breaches.

The incidents can be viewed "as evidence for the importance of AI alignment to ensure models operate predictably," they write, but also "as an irresponsible lapse in standard cybersecurity practices, preventable with stronger sandboxes and procedures." Both fixes are needed.
When models do have internet access, companies need to weigh how much autonomy to grant them.

The letter warns that "the range of model actions permitted by a containment system needs to be balanced with our currently limited ability to predict that the model's actions will not result in a security failure." A model might simply pursue goals its developers never intended, and predicting when that happens remains beyond current capabilities.

The letter calls for an international body that works with governments and specialists from both AI and cybersecurity to set binding standards for any containment approach that allows more external access than airgapping.
This body would also track breakout incidents and require companies to report security failures.
Those reports would later be made public "for both learning and accountability purposes."
Even full airgapping doesn't guarantee safety.

OpenAI researcher Noam Brown recently pointed out that two physically separated computers could theoretically still communicate through temperature sensors, with one heating up its CPU while the other detects the change.
Measures like airgapping or monitoring chains of thought buy time, Brown says, but the alignment problem still needs to be solved.

items.originalTitle: Swinburne and IQM Partner on Quantum Research and Workforce Development
items.summary: Insider Brief Swinburne University of Technology and IQM Quantum Computers have formed a partnership to advance quantum research, technology development, education, and workforce training across Australia, Europe, and the Indo-Pacific. The collaboration will include joint training programs, internships, research projects, technology development, workshops, and exchanges for students, researchers, and staff.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Swinburne University of Technology and IQM Quantum Computers have formed a partnership to advance quantum research, technology development, education, and workforce training across Australia, Europe, and the Indo-Pacific.
The collaboration will include joint training programs, internships, research projects, technology development, workshops, and exchanges for students, researchers, and staff.

The partnership builds on complementary expertise in quantum theory, experimentation, and superconducting quantum computers, with Swinburne representatives visiting IQM ’s production facility in Espoo, Finland.

PRESS RELEASE — Swinburne University of Technology and IQM Quantum Computers , the global leader in superconducting quantum computers, are partnering to advance quantum science, technology, innovation and workforce development capability.
This new partnership will include collaborating in education, training, research engagement and technology development across Australia, Europe and the Indo-Pacific.

“Quantum technologies have the potential to transform industries and address some of the world’s most complex challenges,” says Swinburne ’s Deputy Vice-Chancellor, Research, Professor Karen Hapgood .

“This partnership with IQM reflects our shared commitment to strengthen quantum expertise, expand learning opportunities and support the growth of a skilled workforce.” The development of quantum technologies is a key priority for both Australia and Finland, and this partnership helps to foster the international pathway for collaboration.

Swinburne ‘s quantum expertise in theory and experimentation along with IQM ‘s reputation in producing working quantum computers, will not only enable technology uplift, but will also advance quantum talent in both countries.
“Australia and Finland are both building real quantum capability, not just talking about it,” said IQM ‘s Chief Global Affairs Officer and co-founder, Juha Vartiainen.

In addition, the partnership will also support collaborative research, technology translation and innovation, as well as staff, researcher and student exchanges between Swinburne and IQM , helping to advance the next generation of quantum talent.
The partnership was finalised after a delegation from Swinburne , representing Australia, attended the Finnish Quantum Days event in Jyväskylä, Finland.

evidenceRecords.text: Google is making Gemini 4 Argon available worldwide through its API, the Gemini app, and Google Antigravity.
Internally, Google says Argon already cut coding tasks from months to weeks.
The article Gemini 4 Argon is now available worldwide as Google's most capable frontier model appeared first on The Decoder .
Google is rolling out Gemini 4 Argon globally, making its new flagship AI model available to developers, businesses, and consumers starting today.
Gemini 4 Argon is accessible through the API in AI Studio and the Gemini platform, according to Google.
Google AI Ultra subscribers can use the model in Google Antigravity, while AI Ultra and Pro subscribers get access through the Gemini app and Google Search's AI mode.
Free Gemini users and paying Plus subscribers now only have access to the weaker Flash models under a new model tier structure.
Argon replaces the Gemini Pro class as Google's new frontier series.
Google says more Gemini 4 models will follow, which likely means updated Flash variants that would eventually trickle down to free and Plus users as well.
Internally, Google is reportedly already testing a potential successor codenamed "Carbon," which is supposed to outperform Argon at coding in particular.
Pricing and benchmark results remain as previously reported: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens at the introductory rate, with a 95 percent discount on cached inputs.
Argon holds the top spot on the Vals Index, but it still trails Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 in independent overall rankings.
And because Google waited roughly two weeks to ship, it now also sits behind Meta's Muse Wonder Full, which launched just yesterday.

items.originalTitle: New Data from the Juno Spacecraft Reveals that Jupiter's Has a Rippling, Wavy Magnetodisk
items.summary: Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System and has a planetary magnetosphere to match! Since 2016, NASA's Juno probe has studied this massive planet to better understand its magnetosphere and its famous interaction with Io, its volcanic, innermost moon. evidenceRecords.text: Using observations from NASA's Juno spacecraft, an international team led by Shandong University shows that Jupiter's magnetodisk is a rippling structure that rotates with the planet, contrary to what scientists previously thought.
Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System and has a planetary magnetosphere to match!
Since 2016, NASA's Juno probe has studied this massive planet to better understand its magnetosphere and its famous interaction with Io, its volcanic, innermost moon.
Of particular interest is the ring-shaped magnetodisk, driven by the planet's rapid rotation and Io's volcanic material.
Until recently, scientists pictured this feature as a smooth disk that rises and falls with Jupiter's rotation.
However, an international team led by researchers from Shandong University is changing that view based on new Juno probe data.

As part of their study, which appeared in the journal Science China Earth Sciences, they analyzed Jupiter's magnetic field and energetic particle activity during multiple events in the Jovian magnetodisk.
Their results show that Jupiter's magnetodisk crumples into a wave-like structure during active periods.
Normally, the Juno spacecraft crosses the magnetodisk's current sheet twice per rotation (every 9.9 hours).

Instead, Juno crossed the current sheet repeatedly during magnetodisk reconnection events and detected the same clear magnetic signature (along with bursts of energized electrons and ions) almost every time.
The team's analysis of the current sheet's orientation showed that it doesn't simply rise and fall, but moves like a wave with ripples lasting several minutes to over an hour.
Illustration of Jupiter's magnetodisk current sheet (blue surface), deformed into a rippling structure by numerous small-scale magnetic reconnection sites (yellow speckles).
Credit ©: Science China Press
On Earth, the kink wave moves away from a reconnection site, whereas Jupiter's reconnection signatures point to a rotating, rippled current sheet.
Based on this new data, these particles could complicate the link between the planet's ionosphere and magnetodisk.
In short, their analysis shows that the Jovian magnetodisk is not a simple rotating sheet, but a highly structured, dynamic environment.
The probe continues to fulfill science objectives that build on the findings of NASA's Galileo probe, the only other spacecraft focused exclusively on exploring Jupiter.

items.title: Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case
items.originalTitle: Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case
items.summary: A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July. Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI’s interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI’s first hardware device.

evidenceRecords.text: A federal judge ruled that Apple can access OpenAI's interview materials involving former Apple employees, as well as private messages and testimony from key figures in the case.
A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July.

Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI’s interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI’s first hardware device.

These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components.

The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited.

The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services.

In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data.
Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations.
U.S. District Judge Edward Davila didn’t greenlight all of Apple’s requests for expedited access to OpenAI documents and messages relevant to the case.

But he did rule that Apple could access the interview materials, alongside private LINE messages (from a messaging app) between individuals named in the case, including OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng.
The judge also approved depositions for Liu and Peng, along with a third individual, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer, Tang Yew Tan.
All three are former Apple employees.

items.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
items.originalTitle: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
items.summary: “Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.” Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.

evidenceRecords.text: University of Michigan spinout Laplace Intelligence uses AI agents and interactive simulation to stress-test robots and self-driving vehicles before deployment.

“Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.”
Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI.
The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.
Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15.
It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon, October 13.
Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan.
Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation.
In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature.
That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas.

Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision.
“We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said.

Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them.

While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world.

Of course, for an AI chipmaker, the vision of a home AI appliance, or at least widespread consumer adoption of agentic technology, is certainly appealing.

While AI is already doing many of the things we used to do manually, Feldman is most excited about the new possibilities — things that weren’t possible before.

items.originalTitle: Industrial Next wants factory robots to switch tasks in minutes, not weeks
items.summary: Pankau notes that traditional industrial robots are typically programmed to perform highly specific, repeatable tasks. As a result, even a small change in the process or product can cause the robot to fail or trigger costly downtime, which forces manufacturers to simplify their products for repeatability. evidenceRecords.text: Pankau notes that traditional industrial robots are typically programmed to perform highly specific, repeatable tasks.
As a result, even a small change in the process or product can cause the robot to fail or trigger costly downtime, which forces manufacturers to simplify their products for repeatability.
Making robots truly flexible presents a different challenge.
They need enormous amounts of training data and, unlike AI models trained on the internet, robotics lacks the vast datasets needed to teach machines how to perform complex physical tasks.
“We can make robots do all these cool things like dance around, because there’s data for that, but we can’t make them assemble high-precision things,” Pankau explained.

The secret sauce for the robots that we have is that we have given them an understanding of the process in general, but we build that understanding using an extremely high-fidelity simulation engine that is close to the real dynamics to where we can let the robot do these kinds of high precision tasks almost without seeing the parts at all.”
In other words, the robots practice in a highly detailed virtual world that closely mimics real-world physics.
Industrial Next’s robotic stations can be reconfigured, combined, and redeployed across product lines.
New tasks are taught through simulation and demonstration, rather than hard-coded scripts.

They handle tasks that manufacturers had tried and failed to automate for years, such as threading a delicate flex cable and snapping a tiny connector cap into place. (He wasn’t at liberty to disclose the customer.) He also described a “film peeling” station, where their AI-powered robots strip protective film off camera modules and buttons at or above human speed with 100% accuracy, even when moved to a new phone model and production line they have never seen.

“We started this company because that is the kind of performance that we wish we had at Tesla, where we were bypassing robot stations because we couldn’t program them effectively enough using traditional technologies,” Pankau said. “Now we want to take this to more complicated tasks than just building a phone.
We ultimately want to take this to building a full car end-to-end without any human touching ever.”

items.originalTitle: Quantum Design Oxford Announces Winner of the 2026 Nicholas Kurti Science Prize
items.summary: Insider Brief Dr. Chunyu Guo, a research group leader at the Max Planck Institute for the Structure and Dynamics of Matter, has received the 2026 Nicholas Kurti Science Prize for his research on quantum materials. Guo’s work examines quantum behaviour in kagome metals, including many-body quantum interference, long-range coherent charge transport, and electronic order under extreme conditions. The prize, awarded by Quantum Design Oxford , includes €15,000 and support to attend a global physics conference.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Dr. Chunyu Guo, a research group leader at the Max Planck Institute for the Structure and Dynamics of Matter, has received the 2026 Nicholas Kurti Science Prize for his research on quantum materials.
Guo’s work examines quantum behaviour in kagome metals, including many-body quantum interference, long-range coherent charge transport, and electronic order under extreme conditions.
The prize, awarded by Quantum Design Oxford , includes €15,000 and support to attend a global physics conference.

PRESS RELEASE — Quantum Design Oxford today announces that Dr Chunyu Guo , W2 Research Group Leader at the Max Planck Institute for the Structure and Dynamics of Matter , Hamburg, Germany has been awarded the 2026 Nicholas Kurti Science Prize .

The Award recognises Dr Guo’s contributions to understanding the quantum behaviour of kagome metals and his discovery of many-body quantum interference and long-range coherent charge transport in strain-minimised microstructures under high magnetic fields.
“I am truly honored to receive the Nicholas Kurti Science Prize and to join its distinguished group of past recipients.

Matthew Martin, Managing Director at Quantum Design Oxford , said, “It is always an absolute pleasure to award the Nicholas Kurti prize, and we at Quantum Design Oxford are proud to support young scientists such as Dr Guo.

His work exemplifies the spirit of this prize, and underpins the importance of curiosity-driven and conceptually bold research in advancing the field of quantum materials science and condensed matter physics.” The Nicholas Kurti Science Prize for Europe promotes and recognises the novel work of young scientists working in the fields of low temperatures and/or high magnetic fields or surface science.
The 2026 Nicholas Kurti Science Prize selection committee is co-chaired by Professor Richard Haley (Lancaster University) and Dr Natalia Ares (University of Oxford).
